name: Incisionless Fritsch otoplasty

card.summary: Ear pinning with needle-placed stitches through the skin and no incision; documented, but outcome data are thin.
card.note: Described as suited to milder cases; few outcome data located.

quick.overview:
Incisionless otoplasty reshapes the ear using sutures passed through the skin by needle, avoiding a cut behind the ear. Fritsch published on it between 1995 and 2009.

Sources are brief.
quick.mechanism: Percutaneous sutures fold the antihelix and set back the concha, sometimes with scoring.
quick.risks: No technique-specific studies were found; general otoplasty risks apply, and sources describe it as suited to mild to moderate prominence.

lead: Incisionless (percutaneous) otoplasty, associated with the surgeon Fritsch, is an ear-pinning technique that pulls prominent ears closer to the head by passing sutures through the skin with needles to shape the antihelix and conchal bowl, without cutting the skin open. For people with ears that stick out, the aim is a natural-looking fold and ears that sit closer to the head with a smaller scar footprint and quicker recovery.[1][2]

Wikipedia dates Fritsch's publications on the method from 1995 to 2009 and notes that it is combined with superficial scoring of the front of the cartilage so it bends into the desired shape.[1] It is one of several suture-based techniques, alongside the open Mustardé method and the closed Merck stitch method, with more invasive cartilage-cutting techniques reserved for more severe cases.[1]

Published studies include a retrospective study of 32 children and a comparison of 49 children with and without cartilage scoring; a 2025 review concludes that the technique is effective with shorter recovery and less morbidity when correctly indicated.[2][3][4]

chain: Needle-placed sutures through the skin fold the antihelix and concha
Cartilage is held in a corrected fold with no incision
Ears sit closer to the head with a more natural contour
angle.text: The procedure pins back protruding ears by creating the missing fold with sutures through the skin, so the ears sit closer to the head. It is used for mild to moderate prominence, with no incision scar behind the ear.

paras: Per Wikipedia, needle-placed sutures through the skin shape the antihelix and concha, sometimes with superficial scoring of the cartilage.[1] Grokipedia says incisionless approaches suit mild to moderate prominence.[5] Wikipedia lists otoplasty candidates as people with prominent ears and with congenital or injury-related ear shape problems, with severe prominence sometimes treated in early childhood around age 4.[1]

General otoplasty recovery described by Wikipedia involves swelling and bruising that usually fade within about two weeks, a light dressing for several days, then a snug headband while sleeping for 3 to 6 weeks to keep ears from folding forward.[1]

Wikipedia lists complications of otoplasty generally as hematoma, infection that can progress to cartilage inflammation, sutures poking through the skin (the most common issue, which can lead to painful granulomas), overcorrection giving an unnatural look, and pressure abrasions from dressings.[1] In the 32-child retrospective series, reported complication rates included infection in 9.7% of ears and blistering in 22.6%, with further otoplasty needed in 8.3% of ears; the authors suggested early redness, swelling and blistering may be specific to the technique.[3]

A retrospective observational study of 32 children (62 ears) treated by one surgeon over nine years reported that the proportion of prominent ears fell from 76.8% to 17.8% on facial measurements and that children rated cosmetic outcomes good in 95% of ears.[3] A comparison of 49 children found auriculocephalic distances 1 to 2 mm greater at six months without cartilage scoring, no significant difference in satisfaction or aesthetic ratings, recurrence of 9.1% without scoring and 4.3% with scoring, and the authors concluded scoring was not mandatory in children with soft cartilage.[4] A 2025 review in Facial Plastic Surgery concludes that the technique is effective, with shorter recovery and less morbidity than open techniques when correctly indicated, and stresses thorough preoperative evaluation.[2]

timeline.event: Fritsch publishes on the incisionless otoplasty method.[1]
Study of cartilage scoring in incisionless otoplasty in 49 children published.[4]
Retrospective outcome study of 32 children published.[3]
Review of incisionless otoplasty published in Facial Plastic Surgery.[2]
